Sayers: Ford ‘Adapted Well’ in 30-Hour Aragon Hypercar Test

Ford’s Hypercar program shifts focus to U.S. following 24-plus hours of running at Aragon…

  • by

    Dylan Spaulding
  • November 24, 2026

Photo: Drew Gibson/Ford

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:40
Instaread

Ford Hypercar program manager Dan Sayers said the team “adapted well” to the challenges encountered during last week’s 30-hour endurance test at Motorland Aragon, which represented a significant step in its preparations for the manufacturer’s top class FIA World Endurance Championship debut next year.

The test marked the conclusion of the program’s European Hypercar testing schedule, with the focus now shifting to the U.S. as Ford enters the final stages of on-track development.

It also marked the introduction of a simultaneous second car testing, following separate testing schedules. Noise restrictions in previous tests at Monza and Imola prevented Ford from running both of its LMDh-based cars at the same time.

While one car undertook the endurance run at Aragon, the other focused on performance and controls development.

Despite an unscheduled engine change interrupting the endurance effort, Sayers was encouraged by the car’s performance during its first extended running session, which yielded more than 24 hours of track time during the targeted 30-hour test.

“We hadn’t done more than about a stint and a half continuous running before this, so it was quite a leap into the unknown, despite it being a fairly well proven chassis from ORECA,” Sayers said during a media call Monday.

“We did have some scheduled stops in there just to take the bodywork off to make sure nothing was untoward that we couldn’t see just as a precaution. They all went well.

“The biggest problem we actually had there, we did have some unscheduled downtime, which was an issue with the cooling system, which did actually result in an engine change at 2:30 a.m.. So not surprisingly, we ran into some issues.

“We learned a huge amount. There were no failures that we were concerned about. The cooling issue was extremely simple, which is probably why it’s even more frustrating.

“All in all, we adapted well, and what I would class as a very successful first endurance test.”

The program’s next outings will take place in the U.S., starting at Circuit of The Americas followed by two tests at Sebring International Raceway.

Sayers said the Aragon test also provided valuable insight into smaller issues that can be addressed ahead of the next phase of development.

“It highlighted, and honestly, the biggest problems we had was a few fixings coming out or coming loose or both,” he said. “I’m not going to say they weren’t critical ones, but nothing actually came off the car.

“But we were lucky enough that in the six-hour scheduled inspections, we had noticed them. We can address them and then the car will go back out. It’s those kind of details that we’re on now.

“It’s not fundamental issues with the car with weaknesses, it’s the details which we know are all so important.

“We update the build books every time we go out because things change. You learn more, you learn where the harnesses rub and where they shouldn’t rub.

“So again, we’ve learned a lot. We’ll prepare the cars slightly differently for the next test, as we do every time.”

The test also gave recently appointed reserve driver Tom Dillmann his first extended opportunity behind the wheel of the Hypercar, following a brief shakedown in one of the cars.

Sayers Impressed with Dillmann’s First Proper Test

All seven drivers were present at Aragon, although illness’ prevented Logan Sargeant from taking part in any running, while Mike Rockenfeller completed a few stints before ending his participation in the test earlier than expected.

Sayers praised Dillmann’s initial contribution to the program, highlighting the Frenchman’s pace and feedback during his first extended opportunity in the car.

“Tom joined us at a shakedown for one of the cars recently as well,” he said. “So he had a very, very short run on a very small track. This was his first time in the car. And I’ve got to say, yeah, pretty impressed.

“He’s very easy to work with. He’s very relaxed. He’s obviously super competent in a prototype car. Straight up to speed, very good feedback.

“In terms of feedback, he’s brought a lot already and it’s one test and we’re keen to get him in the simulator as well so he’ll be in the simulator soon out in Concord, preparing and correlating from previous tests and then we’ll have to see how we work that into next season.

“He’ll certainly be on standby at the track for the longer races but in the shorter ones we might even do some live simulator running at the same time.

“He’s got a lot to bring to this program and, it’s great to have him on board.”

Dylan Spaulding is a Florida-based journalist, broadcaster, and communications professional. A University of South Florida graduate, he has contributed to Sports Illustrated, Athlon Sports, and FanSided, with experience spanning sports journalism, motorsports PR, digital media, photography, and play-by-play broadcasting.

CMP privacy choices

Storage, duration, and usage details

The choices you make with this CMP regarding the purposes and entities will affect how personalized advertising is presented to you. We need to store these choices to respect them on future visits, and they are stored differently based on the type of site or app you're using:
  • For sites, your choices are saved in a cookie named “FCCDCF” for a maximum duration of 390 days.
  • For apps, your choices are saved in device storage prefixed by “IABTCF_”. Your choices will be invalidated after 390 days and overwritten once you make new privacy choices on this app.
  • For accelerated mobile page (AMP) sites, your choices are saved in local storage prefixed by “amp-store”. Your choices will be invalidated after 390 days and overwritten once you make new privacy choices on this site.
